lesson.title: Dictionaries Inside Dictionaries
lesson.summary: A dictionary's values can themselves be dictionaries, which lets you model structured, real-world records like a student's grades in multiple subjects.
lesson.body:
A dictionary value can be any type, including another dictionary. This is nesting, and you have already practiced the same idea with nested lists, where a list held other lists as its elements. Nested dictionaries let you represent data that naturally has more than one level, like a roster of students where each student has several subject grades attached to their name.

students = {
    "Ana": {"math": 90, "science": 85},
    "Ben": {"math": 76, "science": 81}
}
print(students["Ana"]["science"])

This prints 85. The first set of brackets, students["Ana"], reaches into the outer dictionary and returns the inner dictionary belonging to Ana, {"math": 90, "science": 85}. The second set of brackets, ["science"], then reaches into that inner dictionary to pull out 85. Chaining brackets like this always works from the outside in, one level at a time.

students["Ben"]["art"] = 95
print(students["Ben"])

This prints {'math': 76, 'science': 81, 'art': 95}. Assigning to students["Ben"]["art"] first finds Ben's inner dictionary, then adds a brand new key, "art", inside it, exactly the way you would add a key to any ordinary dictionary. The outer dictionary, students, is untouched, only Ben's inner dictionary gained an entry.

for name, subjects in students.items():
    average = sum(subjects.values()) / len(subjects)
    print(name, round(average, 1))

This prints Ana 87.5, then Ben 84.0. The loop uses items() to get each student's name and their inner dictionary of subjects, one pair at a time. For Ana, subjects.values() gives 90 and 85, which sum to 175, divided by len(subjects), which is 2, giving 87.5. For Ben, after the art grade was added, subjects.values() gives 76, 81, and 95, which sum to 252, divided by 3, giving 84.0. This is a good example of why nested dictionaries pay off: keys(), values(), and items() all work the same way at every level, so once you know how to use them on a simple dictionary, you already know how to use them on the inner dictionaries too.
